The skin DNA HPV reservoir is transcriptionally silent

Cross-modality decoupling of HPV presence and activity, tested against Shen et al.’s petabase (Logan) papillomavirus survey

Author

Taavi Päll

Published

July 28, 2026

Code 
library(tidyverse); library(here)
s  <- read_csv(here("dna_rna_triangulation/skin_dna_vs_rna_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
ty <- read_csv(here("dna_rna_triangulation/skin_dna_vs_rna_types.csv"),   show_col_types = FALSE)
gv <- read_csv(here("dna_rna_triangulation/skin_dna_vs_rna_genus.csv"),   show_col_types = FALSE)
topdna  <- ty |> arrange(desc(dna_skin_libs)) |> slice(1:6)
topprod <- ty |> filter(rna_productive > 0) |> arrange(desc(rna_productive)) |> slice(1:6)
fmt_list <- function(x) paste(x, collapse = ", ")

Summary

Our RNA-seq survey argues that cutaneous HPV is present but transcriptionally quiet in most skin. That claim is built entirely on transcription, so a sceptic can ask whether the quiet majority is real or just an artefact of what got sequenced. Here we test it against a completely independent DNA dataset: Shen et al.’s petabase re-mining of the Logan/SRA assembly for papillomavirus L1 (github.com/syueqiao/pvs_in_logan). The two datasets share no libraries (Logan is DNA metagenomes, ours is RNA-seq; the SRR sets are disjoint), so this is a composition comparison, not a per-library join. The result is a clean decoupling of presence from activity: the HPV types that dominate the skin DNA reservoir are the ones that are transcriptionally silent, and the transcriptionally productive types are minor or absent from the DNA reservoir. The quiet majority is not a sampling artefact; it is the genuinely dominant β/γ commensal DNA reservoir. Broadening the DNA reservoir to other body sites (Result 3) recovers the textbook tropism from DNA alone — vaginal is overwhelmingly α mucosal, skin is β/γ commensal, gut is a mixture of both — which validates the composition read-out and confirms the skin reservoir is real. A second RNA-activity axis, the anal transition zone (Result 4), closes the loop: its transcriptome is loudly productive α-HPV (100% of productive libraries were α, HPV16-led), while the cutaneous β types that contaminate anal/gut DNA stay silent — so presence and activity separate by genus and by site.

The two datasets and why they cannot be joined

Shen et al. searched the whole Logan assembly (27 M SRA libraries) for papillomavirus L1 and released per-library RunInfo, a library-to-cluster master table, and a cluster-to-type demarcation. We restrict their set to the 1735 human skin-metagenome libraries that carry HPV (ScientificName = “human skin metagenome” / “skin metagenome”; the SRA structured Body_Site field is essentially unpopulated for these, so the metagenome source label is the tissue key). Because Logan is DNA and our survey is RNA-seq, the two SRR universes are entirely disjoint (0 shared libraries out of 12,200 ours and 8,722 HPV+ theirs). That rules out a per-library DNA-vs-RNA validation but makes Shen a genuinely independent, non-redundant DNA layer. We therefore compare type/genus composition:

  • DNA presence — for each HPV type, the number of skin-metagenome libraries carrying it (Shen).
  • RNA activity — per-type library counts in our curated tiers: presence in unselected skin, and productive infection (warts control_productive plus epidermodysplasia verruciformis EV, the two contexts of genuine late-transcript expression; EV is included so β-HPV, which is productive only in EV, is scored fairly).

Cluster-to-type mapping uses Shen’s best_hit_name (e.g. “human papillomavirus 24”), joined to our type_genus.csv; genus keywords (“Gammapapillomavirus N”) resolve the rest, and only libraries whose cluster is flagged novel/no-hit count toward the novel fraction.

The skin set is selected by SRA ScientificName (“human skin metagenome” / “skin metagenome”), a taxid that is also used by studies swabbing environmental surfaces and non-human animal skin. Those libraries carry shed human corneocytes, so they are real deposition, but they are nobody’s skin. build_skin_run_exclusions.py queries BioSample attributes for every skin run and drops 30 of them (23 Hong Kong transit-surface swabs, PRJNA413474; 4 dairy-farm udder epithelium, PRJNA512046; 3 host = bovine cutaneous wounds, PRJNA636289), leaving 1,938 runs. The exclusion table is written to skin_run_exclusions.tsv and is auditable per run. It does not move the composition (β 55.5 → 55.2 %, γ 40.6 → 40.7 %, α and the novel fraction unchanged, and the list of productive types with zero skin DNA is identical), but it does move per-type ranks: HPV17 loses 22 of 71 libraries (DNA rank 7 → 13) and HPV147 loses 11, so transit-surface deposition was inflating specific β/γ types. Per-type ranks quoted from a pre-exclusion run are not valid.

Result 1 — the genus of the reservoir flips from the genus of activity

The skin DNA reservoir is a β/γ commensal community: 55.2% of HPV+ skin-metagenome libraries carry a Betapapillomavirus and 40.7% a Gammapapillomavirus, against only 6.7% carrying an Alphapapillomavirus (Figure 1 A, left). The transcriptionally productive fraction is the mirror image: it is dominated by Alphapapillomavirus (Figure 1 A, right). The genus that fills the reservoir is not the genus that is active.

A striking side-note: 14.5% of skin-metagenome libraries carry a PV cluster that matches nothing in the reference databases, i.e. a candidate novel type. The cutaneous β/γ reservoir remains substantially under-catalogued even at petabase scale.

Result 2 — presence and activity are decoupled at the type level

Ranking types within each axis makes the decoupling explicit (Figure 1 B). The most DNA-abundant skin types are β/γ commensals that are transcriptionally silent: the top of the DNA ranking is HPV24 (128 libraries), HPV12 (96 libraries), HPV20 (81 libraries), HPV107 (80 libraries), HPV173 (80 libraries), HPV21 (78 libraries), and every one of them has essentially no productive-library signal. Conversely, the productive types are α wart viruses that are DNA-rare or entirely absent from the skin reservoir: HPV11 (14 productive), HPV57 (10 productive), HPV42 (9 productive), HPV2 (8 productive), HPV27 (4 productive), HPV91 (3 productive). The archetypal wart types HPV-MKN1NR, HPV11, HPV14, HPV42, HPV44, HPV47, HPV52, HPV57, HPV6, HPV7, HPV78 have zero detections across all 1735 skin-metagenome libraries.

Of the top 20 types on each axis, only 4 are shared (HPV17, HPV2, HPV20, HPV5), and they are the informative exceptions rather than a counter-example:

  • HPV2 is the single α type that is both a frequent skin DNA resident and productive (the “abundant AND productive” corner in Figure 1 B) — the common-wart virus that also persists as skin flora.
  • HPV5, HPV17, HPV20 are the β EV-types: they are abundant in the DNA reservoir and weakly productive, but their productivity comes from the EV context, i.e. it is drawn from the commensal reservoir rather than decoupled from it.

So the decoupling is genus- and context-specific: α wart productivity is independent of the skin DNA reservoir, whereas the little β productivity that exists (in EV) is sampled from it.

Result 3 — the reservoir across body sites recovers known tropism

Our RNA-seq survey is skin-only (tissue categories: 9,037 skin, no vaginal or gut), so vaginal and gut cannot be given a matched RNA-activity axis. What they can show is the DNA reservoir itself, and comparing it across body sites is a strong internal check: if the petabase reservoir is real signal rather than noise, its genus composition should recover the textbook tropism of the papillomaviruses. It does.

Code 
rg <- read_csv(here("dna_rna_triangulation/reservoir_by_tissue_genus.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
gp <- function(tis, g) round(100 * rg$prop[rg$tissue == tis & rg$genus == g], 1)
nv <- function(tis) round(100 * rg$prop[rg$tissue == tis & rg$genus == "Novel_any"], 1)
nlib <- function(tis) format(rg$n_lib[rg$tissue == tis][1], big.mark = ",")

The three body sites give three distinct, biologically expected reservoirs (Figure 2):

  • Skin is a Betapapillomavirus/Gammapapillomavirus commensal reservoir (β 55.2%, γ 40.7% of detections, α only 6.7%), the same composition analysed above.
  • Vaginal is overwhelmingly Alphapapillomavirus (α 84.5%, β 0.4%, γ 1.3%); its top types are the classic mucosal set (HPV91, 51, 66, 67, 16, 90), mixing high- and low-risk α. This is the textbook mucosal niche, recovered here purely from DNA metagenome assembly.
  • Gut is a mixture: α 30.5%, β 34.6%, γ 15.4%. Its top types interleave mucosal α (HPV16, HPV6, HPV56) with cutaneous β skin types (HPV24, HPV124) — exactly the signature of stool/gut metagenomes picking up both mucosal shedding and perianal-skin commensal β-HPV, the same collection-route contamination independently seen in rectal-swab gut metagenomes (the eluring aging cohort).

The novel-cluster fraction tracks how well each niche is catalogued: 14.5% of skin libraries and 9.6% of gut libraries carry an unclassified PV cluster, versus only 0.2% of vaginal libraries — the mucosal α types are exhaustively described, while the cutaneous β/γ reservoir is not.

That the reservoir cleanly reconstructs the vaginal-α / skin-β/γ tropism from DNA alone validates the composition read-out used in Results 1–2: the skin reservoir’s β/γ dominance and the type-level presence/activity decoupling are not analysis artefacts.

Result 4 — the anal niche: an independent RNA-activity axis

The skin decoupling (Results 1–2) rests on a skin RNA-activity axis; the gut/vaginal comparisons (Result 3) could only show the DNA reservoir, because our RNA survey was skin-only. To close that gap for one of the two sites, we ran the HPV-typing pipeline over the anal/anorectal RNA-seq that the survey had never touched — a small, clean niche (anal squamous-cell-carcinoma lines are rare, so the cell-line burden that dominates cervical RNA is minimal here). This gives a genuine RNA-activity axis for the anal transition zone, to set against the mixed gut DNA reservoir of Result 3.

Code 
ap  <- read_csv(here("dna_rna_triangulation/anorectal_pilot/anal_pilot_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
apt <- read_csv(here("dna_rna_triangulation/anorectal_pilot/anal_productive_types.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
a <- function(k) ap$value[ap$metric == k]
top_prod <- apt |> slice_max(productive_samples, n = 4)

Anal tissue is genuinely HPV-rich, unlike healthy skin. Of 681 libraries typed, 230 were HPV-positive (34%; 37% across the anal-carcinoma studies), an order of magnitude above the 2–4% of primary skin. The 5 cell lines flagged by the curation were all HPV-negative (0 positive), so the signal is clinical tissue, not contamination.

And the activity is overwhelmingly productive α. Of 161 libraries with late (L1/L2 capsid) transcripts — the productive-infection signal — 100% were Alphapapillomavirus, led by HPV16 (91), HPV11 (22), HPV6 (14), HPV18 (7). Every one of the 22 productively-expressed types was α; no β or γ type reached productive expression in a single anal library.

This completes the cross-modality decoupling for a second niche, and it does double duty. First it reinforces the decoupling: the anal transition zone sits directly against perianal skin, so the cutaneous β types that leak into gut/anal DNA metagenomes (Result 3: the gut reservoir was a mixture of mucosal α and cutaneous β such as HPV24 and HPV124) are entirely silent in the anal transcriptome — present in DNA, absent from activity. Second, it supplies a positive control the skin analysis lacked: where the skin story is “present but quiet”, the anal α-HPV is loudly productive (HPV16 alone drove 91 productive libraries), exactly as expected for the HPV16-driven anal carcinoma niche and mirroring the cervix. Presence and activity are decoupled by genus and site: mucosal α is productive where it resides (cervix, anus), cutaneous β/γ is a quiet DNA reservoir wherever it is found (skin, and as contamination in gut/anal DNA).

Caveats

  1. The RNA side samples a different skin. Our curated RNA-seq libraries skew clinical/lesion (warts, EV, cSCC), so RNA skin = 0 for the β commensals partly reflects the scarcity of healthy-skin RNA-seq, not only low β expression. The direction (β/γ present-but-quiet, α productive) is robust and biologically expected, but the magnitude of the “silent” column is inflated by RNA library selection. The clean confirmation would restrict the RNA side to unselected skin.
  2. Composition, not prevalence. DNA counts are numerators among HPV+ skin libraries; there is no all-skin-metagenome denominator, so “HPV24 is frequent” means frequent among HPV+ skin metagenomes.
  3. Subtype-letter matching. A few types differ only by a subtype letter between the two sources (e.g. DNA HPV38B/HPV14D vs RNA HPV38/HPV14) and so fail to join; these appear as Unresolved in the DNA genus or as false zeros. The effect is small and does not touch the α-vs-β/γ contrast.
  4. DNA presence is not activity. Logan L1 recovery scores the presence of the episome, not its transcription; the whole point of the comparison is that these two are different, but it means the DNA axis cannot itself speak to productivity.
  5. The anal axis is a first-pass pilot. Result 4 uses the pipeline’s automatic HPV-positive and productive calls before the per-sample tissue curation that the main skin cohort received; ~82% of the accessions carry a generic tissue label and an anal-carcinoma diagnosis rather than an explicit “anal” tissue field. The α-productive signal is strong and unambiguous, but the exact counts will firm up after tiering.

Conclusion

An orthogonal, DNA-based, whole-SRA survey confirms and sharpens the present-but-quiet thesis: the transcriptionally silent majority of cutaneous HPV is the genuinely dominant β/γ commensal DNA reservoir, not an artefact of RNA sampling, and transcriptional productivity is confined to a distinct, DNA-minor set of α wart types (with EV-β productivity the lone strand drawn from the reservoir). A second niche, the anal transition zone, closes the loop from the other direction: its RNA is loudly productive α-HPV (HPV16-driven), while the cutaneous β types that contaminate anal DNA metagenomes stay silent — so presence and activity separate by genus and by site, not by chance. The reproducible scripts, tables and figures are in this directory (shen_skin_dna_vs_rna.R, shen_reservoir_by_tissue.R, anorectal_pilot/).

What the cervical/vaginal run would add

The anal pilot is the smaller, cleaner half of the mucosal story; the cervical/vaginal set is the larger and more decisive one, and it is the natural next run (../rna_extension_scoping/, ~6,400 new curation-ready libraries). Three things it would resolve that the current work only implies:

  1. The direct vaginal presence-vs-activity test. Result 3 showed the vaginal DNA reservoir is 84% α, dominated by HPV91/51/66/67/16/90. A vaginal RNA-activity axis would ask, for the same tissue, whether those DNA-frequent types are the productive ones — the exact within-tissue join we could only do for skin. The mucosal prediction is that they largely coincide (unlike skin, where DNA-frequent β is silent), which would make the cervix the clean contrast case to skin: a niche where presence does predict activity.
  2. A high-risk vs low-risk activity gradient. With thousands of libraries spanning normal cervix → CIN → carcinoma, the productive signal can be resolved by lesion grade, testing whether high-risk α (HPV16/18/31/33/45) dominate productive expression in disease while low-risk α (HPV6/11) and the many commensal mucosal types stay quiet — the mucosal analogue of the skin β-reservoir story.
  3. A real stress-test of the cell-line curation. Cervical RNA-seq is ~62% cell-line-tripped (HeLa/SiHa/CaSki), versus near-zero for anal. The anal pilot showed the curation cleanly zeroed out its few cell lines; the cervical run is where that machinery earns its keep at scale, and a clean α-productive tissue signal emerging from behind the HeLa wall would be the strongest possible demonstration that the contamination-aware framework works.

The one operational lesson from this pilot: run the cervical set with the per-sample cell-line classifier and the SNP/contamination checks at full strength, and expect the tissue-curation step (not the typing) to be the real work, given how much of the cervical archive is immortalised-line material.
